units.translation: where the sequence of thoughts is inept and some future is required, not the present κοιράνεῖ [he rules]: about which I have said more in Annot. Oxon. p. 255, where I conjectured that the meaning of Aeschylus's words was this: σωθεὶς δ᾽ ἀτίμως τήνδε ποιμανεῖ χθόνα [but saved without honor he will shepherd this land] (or τῆσδε δεσπόσει χθονός [he will be master of this land]).
All things were done (Stanley: brought upon) except to rule over the gods.
but saved equally he will rule this land
but saved without honor he will shepherd this land
he will be master of this land
when the sea sleeps in midday beds, having fallen
let death come before the marriage bed
alas for me, this bed of slavery (you lie)
with favorable fortune (Hermann: with favorable fortune) in bed
you will remove the seeds of the bitter-sweet pomegranate
Zeus is indeed the punisher of overly proud thoughts
the race is glued to ruin
the grace of well-formed statues is hateful to a man
Of the bosom of the sea.
carrying in the bosom of her linen robe
they wet their bosoms with copious tears
whistling without wings in the bosom of the aegis
to the great bosom of Rhea
the Dodonian land and the Melian gulf
in the manner of a diver
he seems likely to drag you by the hair, having torn it out
to take care of, to deem worthy of care
to carry, to bear, to convey
Middle form κομίζομαι, i.e. κομίζω ἐμαυτόν, I betake myself, I withdraw
examples of which meaning collected from Homer and others, see in Thes. vol. 4 p. 1778.
which the scholiast explains as ἀντὶ τοῦ σῶζε ἡμᾶς [instead of "save us"].
of the body of the dead Orestes, i.e. κομίζειν εἰς τοὺς οἴκους [to bring into the house], as the scholiast explains.
about which see Thes. vol. 4 p. 1781.
a paean (thus Blomfield for παιών) – may he bring the newly mixed, dear one
bringing his foot out of the destructive mud
whether the opinion of friends will prevail to bring him, or whether to bury him as a resident alien
bringing courage from sacrifices to dying men
betake yourself as quickly as possible out of my sight
Interpolated reading, for which I restored καρπός ἧς [the fruit of which] (i.e. ὁμιλίας κακῆς [of evil association]) ἀσύμφορος [unprofitable], about which I have spoken in Philologus vol. 16 p. 220.
who will stand without trembling against a boasting man (M: having boasted, with the other reading written above by a later hand)?
as it is likely for him to boast in the light of the sun
I would not boast that I am the best judge of oracles
you boast such a word against a man
